chunks.pageTitle: Alcohol MAT — ED AUD Pharmacotherapy — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: Start in the ED Most EDs never start treatment for alcohol use disorder despite millions of alcohol-related visits. Yet AUD medications are safe, effective, and easy to begin in the ED , and same-visit initiation plus warm referral increases follow-up. A brief SBIRT (Screening, Brief Intervention, Referral to Treatment) takes minutes and reduces drinking and repeat visits. ⚠️ Decision-support summary — verify doses, contraindications, and interactions against current references and your KP SBC ED / Addiction Medicine protocol , and confirm with pharmacy. Not a substitute for clinical judgment.

chunks.pageTitle: Alcohol MAT — ED AUD Pharmacotherapy — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: ⚠️ Treat alcohol withdrawal first. Maintenance AUD medications below are not withdrawal management. Assess withdrawal (e.g., CIWA-Ar) and treat moderate–severe withdrawal with benzodiazepines/phenobarbital per protocol before or alongside starting maintenance pharmacotherapy.

chunks.pageTitle: Alcohol MAT — ED AUD Pharmacotherapy — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: Medication Typical dose Notes / cautions Naltrexone (PO) first-line 50 mg PO daily (some start 25 mg ) Can start while still drinking. Contraindicated with current opioid use/dependence (need ~7–10 opioid-free days) and in acute hepatitis / liver failure ; caution in active liver disease — check LFTs. Naltrexone (IM XR) 380 mg IM every 4 weeks Improves adherence; same opioid/hepatic cautions as oral. Acamprosate 666 mg PO three times daily No hepatic metabolism → good in liver disease and when opioids are needed . Renally cleared: reduce to 333 mg TID if moderate renal impairment; avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30) .

chunks.pageTitle: Alcohol MAT — ED AUD Pharmacotherapy — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: Gabapentin second-line / off-label Per protocol (titrated) May reduce cravings/withdrawal symptoms; consider misuse/dependence potential and renal dosing. Topiramate / Disulfiram Specialist / selected patients Topiramate off-label (titrate, cognitive/teratogenic cautions). Disulfiram only with abstinence commitment + supervision. Pick by comorbidity: liver disease or on opioids → acamprosate ; otherwise naltrexone (esp. if reducing heavy drinking is the goal). Start in the ED and refer for ongoing management.

chunks.pageTitle: Alcohol MAT — ED AUD Pharmacotherapy — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.section: 💬 How to Talk to the Patient
chunks.text: Use SBIRT : screen, give brief feedback, and refer — non-judgmentally, with permission. "Would it be okay if we talked about your drinking for a minute?" "There are medications that reduce cravings and help people cut back or stop — and we can start one today if you're open to it." "This is common and treatable, and I'm not here to judge. What, if anything, worries you about your drinking?" Ask permission; offer clear, nonjudgmental feedback linking the visit to alcohol when relevant. Use person-first language ("person with alcohol use disorder"). Offer a concrete next step (medication today + a referral) rather than only advice to "cut down."

chunks.text: 17 CCR §2606 California has been declared a rabies area in all 58 counties, so under Title 17 CCR §2606 a clinician who treats any bite from a mammal (a species subject to rabies) must report it to the local health officer immediately — regardless of whether the animal appears ill, is vaccinated, or is later found healthy. Reporting triggers the standard 10-day observation / quarantine of the biting animal and the local rabies risk assessment. 📍 Jurisdiction matters: in San Bernardino County, bite reports route to the animal control agency responsible for where the bite occurred .

chunks.pageTitle: Animal Bite / Rabies Reporting — SBC — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: SBC Animal Care covers the unincorporated areas and most contract cities, but some incorporated cities run their own animal control — route to that agency when applicable. ⚠️ Contact details below are compiled from public sources and should be verified against current SBC Animal Care / Public Health guidance and your KP SBC ED policy before relying on them — phone/fax numbers and forms change. The fax number in particular is from a secondary source; confirm before faxing PHI.

If the bite occurred in such a city, report to that city's animal control / police non-emergency line. Confirm the responsible agency for the bite location.

chunks.pageTitle: Animal Bite / Rabies Reporting — SBC — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: Reporting is one piece — also address the clinical bite workup per current guidance: Rabies risk assessment / PEP: evaluate species, provocation, vaccination/observation status, and exposure type; start rabies PEP (RIG + vaccine series) when indicated per CDPH/ACIP. Bats and most wild carnivores are high-risk. Wound care: copious irrigation; consider leaving high-risk wounds open; document neurovascular and tendon exam. Tetanus prophylaxis per status. , cat/human bites, hand/face, puncture, immunocompromised) per local guidance. Animal observation: a healthy dog/cat/ferret can typically be observed 10 days; report so the local health officer can coordinate quarantine.

chunks.section: ❤️ HEART Score — Chest Pain Risk Stratification
chunks.text: Each category scored 0–2. Score ≤3 = low risk (MACE <2%). Use with serial troponins.

chunks.section: ❤️ HEART Score — Chest Pain Risk Stratification
chunks.text: H — History Slightly suspicious — mostly non-specific features 0 Moderately suspicious — features of ACS but not classic +1 Highly suspicious — classic exertional, pressure-type, radiation +2 E — EKG Normal 0 Non-specific repolarization disturbance (LBBB, pacemaker, early repol, LVH, ST depression ≤1mm) +1 Significant ST deviation — ST depression >1mm, new ST elevation, T-wave inversion +2 A — Age Age < 45 0 Age 45–64 +1 Age ≥ 65 +2 R — Risk Factors (HTN, hypercholesterolemia, DM, obesity BMI>30, smoking, family hx, atherosclerosis) No known risk factors 0 1–2 risk factors +1 ≥3 risk factors OR known CAD / atherosclerotic disease +2 T — Troponin (relative to institutional upper limit of normal) ≤ normal limit (≤1× ULN) 0 1–3× ULN +1 >3× ULN +2 — Select all categories above Score each domain to calculate HEART score.

6-week MACE risk (death, MI, revascularization): 0–3 — Low Risk MACE ~1.7%. Eligible for early discharge with outpatient follow-up if serial troponins negative. Shared decision-making discussion documented. 4–6 — Moderate Risk MACE ~12–17%. Consider observation, stress testing, or cardiology consult. Not safe for routine discharge without further evaluation. 7–10 — High Risk MACE ~50–65%. Early invasive strategy indicated. Cardiology consult, admission, likely catheterization. ⚠️ HEART score does not replace clinical judgment. Patients with STEMI, new LBBB, or hemodynamic instability require immediate intervention regardless of score.

chunks.section: PNL Adult Acute Transfusion Reaction — Order Set
chunks.text: Emergency Medicine · Hospital Medicine · Blood Bank · Pathology · FMC & OMC 🩸 Transfusion Reaction Purpose Epic order set (KPHC PNL Adult Acute Transfusion Reaction ) for management of suspected acute transfusion reactions. Contains nursing communication orders for minor vs major reactions plus medication orders for antipyretic, antihistamine, epinephrine, and corticosteroid therapy. 🖼️ Order Set — Epic Screenshot Open Full-Size ↗ ⚠️ Minor vs Major Reactions — Recognition ⚠️ Minor Acute Transfusion Reaction ≤1°C rise in temp above baseline, chills, pruritus, urticaria (with or without hives). Hold or slow transfusion for 15 minutes and check for symptom resolution.

chunks.pageTitle: Hospital Protocols — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.section: PNL Adult Acute Transfusion Reaction — Order Set
chunks.text: If symptoms have resolved, resume transfusion at original rate . Continue to monitor for recurring symptoms. If symptoms persist, notify physician and treat with ordered medication. 🆘 Major Acute Transfusion Reaction Respiratory distress, hemoglobinuria, loss of consciousness, hypertension, hypotension, angioedema, chest pain, flank or back pain, jaundice, abnormal bleeding, or oliguria/anuria. Anesthetized patient: disseminated bleeding or oozing from IV sites may be the only indication of an acute transfusion reaction. Immediately STOP the transfusion. Disconnect the infusion set with the donor unit and normal saline attached. Maintain patent IV site with normal saline.

chunks.pageTitle: Hospital Protocols — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.section: PNL Adult Acute Transfusion Reaction — Order Set
chunks.text: Immediately perform clerical check — compare donor unit, form, and patient wristband. Notify physician and laboratory. Administer epinephrine IM in the anterolateral aspect of the middle third of the thigh for suspected anaphylactic reaction. Draw a STAT EDTA sample , send IMMEDIATELY to lab with completed ISTR paper form (Investigation of Suspected Transfusion Reaction), plus donor unit with attached infusion set and all attached solutions including normal saline. 3 mg, intraMUSCULAR, EVERY 10 MINUTES AS NEEDED for 3 doses Indication: suspected anaphylactic acute transfusion reaction. ⚠️ If 3rd dose is administered, call physician for further orders .

chunks.pageTitle: Hospital Protocols — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.section: PNL Adult Acute Transfusion Reaction — Order Set
chunks.text: 💊 methylPREDNISolone (Solu-MEDROL) 125 mg IV — Severe Transfusion Reaction 125 mg, intraVENOUS, ONE TIME AS NEEDED for 1 dose Indication: severe acute transfusion reaction. ⚠️ Do not administer within 4 hours of a previous dose of methylprednisolone. 🧭 Bedside Quick Flow STOP / SLOW — minor: hold/slow ×15 min; major: stop immediately. KEEP IV OPEN with normal saline (new tubing, do not flush donor blood). CLERICAL CHECK — unit label vs. ISTR form vs. patient wristband. NOTIFY physician + blood bank/lab; complete ISTR paper form . SEND TO LAB — STAT EDTA sample + donor unit + tubing + all attached solutions. 3 mg IM (anaphylaxis) · methylprednisolone 125 mg IV (severe).

chunks.section: Aerogen Ultra Nebulizer — Peds ED Trial
chunks.text: Respiratory Therapy · Pediatrics · Emergency Medicine 🫁 Peds Trial RT is trialing the Aerogen Ultra nebulizer for peds patients in the ED . Because much more medication reaches the lungs with each breath, kids often need fewer treatments — anecdotally just 1–2 instead of the usual 3 back-to-back doses or a continuous neb. ⚙️ How it works A small Aerogen controller box mounted on the headwall drives the nebulizer. Instead of standard continuous, passive flow, the aerosol is carried into the lungs with each breath — so more drug is delivered per breath. Technically a vibrating-mesh nebulizer: the controller vibrates a fine mesh to make the aerosol rather than using gas-jet flow.

chunks.pageTitle: Hospital Protocols — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.section: Aerogen Ultra Nebulizer — Peds ED Trial
chunks.text: Published studies report roughly 6× more drug reaching the lungs vs. a standard jet neb during spontaneous breathing. ✅ Why it helps Fewer continuous nebs and lower admission rates . Very quiet — in practice kids are not scared of it. 💊 How to use it Must be delivered with a mask (use a valved mask for kids under 5; a mouthpiece is most effective for older, cooperative kids). Albuterol dose can still be adjusted as usual. DuoNeb can still be given.

chunks.section: Acute ICH — First Moves in the ED
chunks.text: Initiate the ICH ED order set in Health Connect. Target SBP 130–150 mmHg in the ED (avoid dropping <130 in mild–moderate ICH — see below). Reverse oral anticoagulation rapidly — stop the agent and give the right reversal as soon as possible. Do NOT give levetiracetam (Keppra) to all ICH patients — only for confirmed/suspected seizure. Call early per the Neuro Hub pathway for vascular neurology / neurosurgery input. Decision-support only. Adapted from the 2026 ICH Update — SBC ED Education (N. , Stroke 2022). chunks.pageTitle: ICH Protocol — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: 🩸 Lowering BP in Acute ICH Mild–moderate ICH presenting with SBP 150–220 → acutely lower to a target of 140 , maintaining 130–150 . COR 2b Start treatment within 2 h of onset and reach target within 1 h to reduce hematoma expansion. COR 2a Titrate for smooth, sustained control — avoid peaks and large SBP variability. COR 2a Large/severe ICH or those needing surgical decompression → safety/efficacy of intensive lowering is not well established . COR 2b If mild–moderate ICH presenting with SBP >150 , acutely lowering to <130 is potentially harmful . 3: Harm Goal in the ED: SBP 130–150. , nicardipine (Cardene) or clevidipine (Cleviprex) infusion) for smooth control.

chunks.pageTitle: Neuro Hub — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: 🏥 What Is the Neuro Hub? The Regional Neuro Hub is the primary triage and consultation point for all Intracerebral Hemorrhage (ICH) cases at this facility and affiliated sites — excluding LAMC, which has its own neurosurgical coverage. The Hub is staffed by Regional Vascular Neurology and exists to: → Standardize acute ICH management across the network → Optimize ICU capacity utilization → Reduce unnecessary or premature neurosurgical transfers → Provide real-time guidance on BP targets, reversal agents, and osmotherapy ⚠️ Site Exclusion: LAMC patients are excluded from this protocol. All other ED and Hospitalist sites route ICH through this Hub before any neurosurgical contact.

chunks.pageTitle: Neuro Hub — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: 📞 Primary Contact — ETAP Line 866-361-2911 Available during all operational hours · ~5 min callback guaranteed 🕐 Standard Operational Hours 1:00 PM – 9:00 PM 7 Days/Week · Including Weekends & Holidays

chunks.pageTitle: Neuro Hub — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.section: Do NOT Page Neurosurgery Directly for ICH
chunks.text: All ICH cases — regardless of size, location, or perceived severity — must be triaged through the Regional Vascular Neurology team via the ETAP line first. The Neuro Hub neurologist will determine whether surgical escalation is warranted and will initiate neurosurgery contact internally if needed. Bypassing this step delays standardized care, disrupts triage flow, and may result in inappropriate or premature surgical referrals. One call. One number. Every time: 866-361-2911

chunks.pageTitle: Opioid MAT — ED Buprenorphine (OUD) — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: MAT Act 2023 · No X-waiver ED-initiated buprenorphine roughly doubles engagement in addiction treatment at 30 days and reduces overdose death. Since the X-waiver was eliminated (MAT Act, Consolidated Appropriations Act 2023) , any clinician with a standard DEA registration (Schedule III) may prescribe buprenorphine for OUD — no special waiver, no patient cap . California's CA Bridge model (buprenorphine + a substance-use navigator + take-home naloxone) is the statewide standard this page summarizes. ⚠️ Decision-support summary of the CA Bridge protocol — verify against current CA Bridge guidance and your KP SBC ED / Addiction Medicine protocol before use.

chunks.pageTitle: Opioid MAT — ED Buprenorphine (OUD) — KP SBC ED Toolkit

chunks.pageTitle: Opioid MAT — ED Buprenorphine (OUD) — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: ⚠️ Precipitated withdrawal risk. For observed/standard induction, wait until the patient is in objective opioid withdrawal — COWS ≥ 8 — before the first dose. High potency fentanyl complicates timing; consider low-dose ("micro") induction or specialist input when standard timing is difficult. Target ~8 mg day 1, up to 16 mg (some protocols to 32 mg ). Start low, go slow Borderline COWS 8–9 or apprehensive 2 mg SL, then 2–4 mg every 1–2 h to effect. , 16 mg ) with reassessment — per CA Bridge high-dose guidance.

chunks.pageTitle: Opioid MAT — ED Buprenorphine (OUD) — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: No X-waiver needed — prescribe buprenorphine/naloxone SL to bridge to the first clinic visit (e.g., a few days to ~1–2 weeks' supply per protocol). Warm handoff: connect to a substance-use navigator / bridge clinic and addiction medicine before discharge (see referral lines below). Take-home naloxone for every OUD patient and their household — see harm reduction. Document OUD, withdrawal (COWS), shared decision-making, and follow-up plan.

chunks.pageTitle: Opioid MAT — ED Buprenorphine (OUD) — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: Take-home naloxone (intranasal 4 mg ): prescribe/dispense and teach the patient + family how to use it; furnishable without an individual Rx under California's standing order. Overdose education: don't use alone, go slow with new supply, fentanyl is in most of the supply. Fentanyl/xylazine test strips and safer-use supplies where available. Meet patients where they are — offer naloxone and follow-up even if they decline medication today .

chunks.pageTitle: Opioid MAT — ED Buprenorphine (OUD) — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.section: 💬 How to Talk to the Patient
chunks.text: Brief, non-judgmental, and hopeful. Use motivational interviewing and person-first language ("person with opioid use disorder," not "addict"; "positive/negative" not "clean/dirty"). "We have a medication called buprenorphine that treats opioid use disorder. It eases withdrawal and cravings, and it cuts the risk of overdose death. " "This is a medical condition, not a moral failing — and it's treatable. " Ask permission to discuss; affirm any step toward safety. Normalize relapse as part of a chronic condition; avoid ultimatums. Emphasize "you can start today" — same-visit initiation is a key driver of follow-up.

chunks.pageTitle: Peds Fever — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: 🔴 ALL febrile 0–6 day infants = HIGHEST RISK — Always admit This is the most vulnerable age band. All febrile infants 0–6 days admit for full workup , parenteral antibiotics, and HSV evaluation regardless of how well they look. Vertically-transmitted infections (HSV, GBS, Listeria, E. coli) dominate; sepsis can present without classic systemic signs. 5 (Fitzwater, 9/10/2025) — this age band is not in the original AAP 2021 CPG or KP NorCal CA FIRST and is sourced directly from the KP-SoCal protocol. 5 decision flow (0–6 days) Every patient → Admission.

chunks.pageTitle: Peds Fever — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: Workup intensity depends on the clinical picture: Ill-appearing OR high-risk infant: Full workup (Urine + Blood + CSF + HSV) · Antibiotics yes · Consider acyclovir. Well-appearing AND not high-risk: Urine + Blood baseline. 5°C → add CSF + HSV : CSF positive → Admit · consider HSV based on risk · antibiotics + consider acyclovir. CSF negative, UA / CBC positive → Admit · no further labs · antibiotics yes , consider acyclovir. CSF negative, UA / CBC negative → Admit · no further labs · consider withholding antibiotics . 5°C → Admit for observation; CSF only if antibiotics are to be given; consider withholding antibiotics .

chunks.pageTitle: Peds Fever — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: "High-risk infant" criteria (any one): prematurity <37 wk (well-appearing 35–36 wk GA may not be high-risk if no other RFs) · perinatal maternal fever / infection / antibiotics, excluding GBS prophylaxis (only counts if infant <14 days old) · neonatal surgery / infection · immune compromise · congenital or chromosomal anomaly · technology-dependent / medically fragile · HSV history or exam (vesicles, seizures, mucous-membrane ulcers, maternal genital HSV). Terminology — "Consider" : management depends on patient circumstances (height of fever, duration of fever, severity of other risk factors). A pediatrics consult may be helpful.

chunks.text: 🧫 HSV — Lower threshold at this age → Full HSV workup + empiric IV acyclovir when any of the following are present: Maternal genital HSV lesions OR maternal fever 48 h before/after delivery Vesicles · seizures · mucous-membrane ulcers · hypothermia CSF pleocytosis with negative Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia Elevated ALT in an infant <29 days old — by itself a trigger to complete a full HSV workup and start acyclovir Definitions of positive labs: Positive UA = + LE on dipstick OR >5 WBC/HPF (centrifuged) OR >10 WBC/mm³ (uncentrifuged). Positive CBC = WBC <5,000 OR >15,000 OR bands >1,500. Positive CSF = WBC with pleocytosis for age, OR traumatic tap.

chunks.text: Surgery · Emergency Medicine · Infectious Disease 🔴 Transfer / Surgical necrotizing fasciitis soft tissue infection surgical emergency LRINEC score time-critical Summary Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening bacterial infection of the fascial planes that requires immediate surgical consultation and debridement — delays of even a few hours significantly increase mortality. Diagnosis is primarily clinical (severe pain out of proportion to exam, woody induration, crepitus, skin necrosis), supported by CT showing gas tracking along fascial planes and a LRINEC score ≥6, though a low score does not exclude the diagnosis.

chunks.pageTitle: Service Agreements — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: Management in the ED centers on broad-spectrum antibiotics (Vancomycin + Pip-Tazo ± Clindamycin), aggressive IV resuscitation, and emergent surgical referral; if surgical capability is unavailable on-site, initiate treatment and transfer without delay. chunks.text: Pediatrics · Pediatric Surgery · Emergency Medicine 🟣 Peds Surgery Consult appendicitis pediatric peds surgery abdominal pain PAS score GMC → STMC transfer Summary This agreement outlines the collaborative pathway between the Emergency Department and Pediatric Surgery for children (ages 0–13) presenting with suspected appendicitis at a GMC without an inpatient pediatric floor. The local Surgeon on Duty (SOD) is called first to confirm suspected appendicitis, then contacts PTAC to coordinate surgeon-to-surgeon transfer to the STMC — with age determining the accepting surgical service (Pediatric Surgery for ages 0–5, Adult General Surgery for ages 6–13).

chunks.pageTitle: Service Agreements — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: If the local SOD is unavailable and CT confirms appendicitis, the ED physician may initiate transfer directly through PTAC. The Pediatric Appendicitis Score (PAS ≥7 highly suspicious, <5 less likely) and pediatric CT protocol guide imaging decisions, and the accepting surgeon creates an OR case at STMC immediately upon transfer confirmation to reduce time to surgery. chunks.pageTitle: Service Agreements — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: Urology · Emergency Medicine 🩺 Tiered Consult urology renal stone hematuria urinary retention 4-tier pathway torsion Fournier's gangrene Summary This agreement defines a four-tier ED disposition pathway for urologic conditions: Tier 1 (call Urology immediately) covers true emergencies such as testicular torsion, persistent priapism, penile fracture, Fournier's gangrene, obstructing stone with fever >38°C, and refractory gross hematuria; Tier 2 (admit to Hospital Medicine, no overnight Urology call 7 PM–7 AM) applies to non-febrile obstructive stone pain, controlled hematuria on CBI, and septic epididymo-orchitis without abscess; Tier 3 (outpatient Urology referral, no ED consult) covers stones >3 mm without fever, successful urinary retention with Foley placed, incidental renal masses, and testicular masses on ultrasound; Tier 4 (PCP follow-up only) applies to stones ≤3 mm without fever, uncomplicated UTI/pyelonephritis, balanitis, and benign hydroceles.

chunks.pageTitle: Service Agreements — KP SBC ED Toolkit

chunks.text: Orthopedics · Internal Medicine · Emergency Medicine 🦴 Dual Consult Required hip fracture orthopedics internal medicine admit surgical planning Summary Once a hip fracture patient arrives in the ED, both Medicine and Orthopedics are to be consulted simultaneously — Medicine to arrange admission and Orthopedics to begin expedited surgical planning. This dual-consult approach has been shown to move patients out of the ED sooner, reduce time to surgery, decrease medical complications, shorten overall length of stay, and free up hospital beds for other patients.

chunks.text: Internal Medicine · General Surgery · Emergency Medicine 🟡 Routing Agreement biliary disease bowel obstruction diverticulitis post-op complications IM vs Gen Surg trauma Summary This agreement defines which service admits for common surgical presentations: biliary disease with confirmed gallstones (acute cholecystitis, gallstone pancreatitis, choledocholithiasis with cholelithiasis) goes to General Surgery, while biliary pathology without gallstones, post-cholecystectomy stones, or surgical refusal goes to Internal Medicine.

chunks.pageTitle: Service Agreements — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: Bowel obstruction with an incarcerated hernia or CT transition zone goes to General Surgery; ileus, carcinomatosis, impaction, or refusal of surgery goes to Internal Medicine. For diverticulitis, free air or abscess requiring intervention goes to General Surgery; all other cases go to Internal Medicine. Any post-operative complication (wound infection, dehiscence, abscess) goes to General Surgery, while non-surgical post-op issues (PE/DVT, pneumonia, MI/CHF) go to Internal Medicine. Necrotizing fasciitis and large abscesses requiring surgery go to General Surgery; all other cellulitis goes to Internal Medicine.

chunks.pageTitle: Service Agreements — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: For trauma, multisystem or wound-care cases go to General Surgery, while patients transferred from outside hospitals with only active medical issues go to Internal Medicine. chunks.section: OB/L&D — Viable Pregnancy Transfer from ED
chunks.text: OB-GYN · Labor & Delivery · Emergency Medicine · FMC (OMC mirroring) 🟣 Transfer Policy Summary ED patients with a viable pregnancy who need monitoring should be sent to Labor & Delivery — not discharged from the ED first. Discharging from the ED ends the encounter and forces L&D to re-register the patient, which was the root cause of recent workflow confusion. This is the current FMC policy; OMC is mirroring the same process. Key rule Do NOT discharge a viable-pregnancy patient from the ED when transferring to L&D for monitoring. Keep them on the ED trackboard until L&D takes over. How the handoff works ED identifies a viable-pregnancy patient needing L&D monitoring.

chunks.pageTitle: Service Agreements — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.section: OB/L&D — Viable Pregnancy Transfer from ED
chunks.text: Patient is physically moved to L&D while still on the ED trackboard / encounter. When the patient arrives in L&D, the L&D clerk calls down to the ED . ED then removes the patient from the trackboard, which allows L&D to create the new encounter. Why Discharging from the ED first closes the encounter and can cause the patient to be lost to the L&D workflow. Keeping the ED encounter open until L&D confirms arrival preserves continuity of care and documentation. Source David Kim / Mike Schwartzwald · Mar 19–20, 2026 · internal clarification thread (FMC policy; OMC mirroring)

chunks.text: Vertigo Helper — KP SBC ED Toolkit Clinical Disclaimer: This tool is a decision-support aid only and does not replace physician assessment. Always apply clinical judgment. Based on GRACE-3 guidelines and expert consensus.

chunks.pageTitle: Vertigo Helper — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.section: Step 1 — Screen for Central Features (Red Flags)
chunks.text: 1 Red Flag Screening Check all that apply. If any are present, a central cause is suspected. Focal weakness or paresthesia (face or limbs) Any of the "Deadly D's": Diplopia, Dysarthria, Dysmetria, Dysphonia, Dysphagia i The Deadly D's Diplopia — double vision Dysarthria — slurred speech Dysmetria — inability to judge distance/scale of movement Dysphonia — difficulty producing voice Dysphagia — difficulty swallowing Inability to stand or walk unaided (new onset) Spontaneous purely vertical or torsional nystagmus at rest New significant, sustained headache or neck pain

chunks.pageTitle: Vertigo Helper — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: Stroke, hemorrhage, or dissection must be ruled out. Do not proceed with peripheral vertigo workup. Activate stroke protocol Emergent CT/CTA head and neck Consider MRI with DWI if available and patient is stable Neurology / stroke team consultation Monitor for clinical deterioration None of the above — Proceed to Step 2 →

chunks.pageTitle: Vertigo Helper — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: 2 Timing, Triggers & Nystagmus Select the category that best matches the patient's presentation. Vertigo Pattern A — Triggered Episodic Vertigo (t-EVS / BPPV likely) Short episodes (<2 min), initiated by head movement (e.g., rolling in bed), no nystagmus at rest B — Acute Vestibular Syndrome (AVS) Constant, ongoing vertigo (hours to days), worsened by head movement, with spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus at rest C — Acute Imbalance Constant dizziness, but no nystagmus at rest

chunks.pageTitle: Vertigo Helper — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: Perform Dix-Hallpike Test i Dix-Hallpike Maneuver 1. Patient seated, turn head 45° to one side 2. Rapidly lower to supine with head hanging 20° off table edge 3. Observe eyes for upbeat-torsional nystagmus (latency 2–10s, fatigues in <60s) 4. Positive = affected side is the downward ear 5. Repeat for opposite side if first negative Positive Dix-Hallpike → Diagnosis: Posterior Canal BPPV Treatment: Perform Epley Maneuver (canalith repositioning). Discharge with return precautions. ⚠️ Do NOT perform the HINTS exam for this category. HINTS is validated only for Acute Vestibular Syndrome (constant vertigo with nystagmus at rest).

chunks.pageTitle: Vertigo Helper — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: In episodic positional vertigo, HINTS results are unreliable and may be falsely reassuring. CT scan is also not indicated for isolated BPPV.

chunks.pageTitle: Vertigo Helper — KP SBC ED Toolkit
chunks.text: ! Gait Assessment Patient has constant dizziness without nystagmus. Assess for objective gait instability. Gait Finding Objective new difficulty walking / Cannot walk unaided Normal gait

Use attending-level escalation when classification is uncertain or condition is worsening. Hospital Medicine admit without overnight Urology call (7 PM-7 AM) for defined intermediate-risk scenarios. Outpatient Urology referral for stable stone/mass/retention categories not requiring emergent intervention.
